deep.reconstruction:
This page is from Euler's 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina', Caput I (E792, Opera Posthuma, Arithmetica, p. 4). It is an elementary, axiomatic-style build-up of divisibility and multiplication from the definition 'number = multitude of units'. Throughout, numbers are positive integers.

§13. The multiples of a are 2a, 3a, 4a, .... (In §11 a itself is called the 'simplum'.) No number in {1, 2, ..., a-1} is a multiple of a. Between any multiple ka and the next one (k+1)a there are again exactly a-1 non-multiples: ka+1, ..., ka+a-1.

§14. Let 1 <= α < a. Then α, a+α, 2a+α, 3a+α, ... are not multiples of a. Implicit reason (mine): ka < ka+α < (k+1)a, so the number lies strictly between consecutive multiples.

§15. Since α < a, we have a < 2a-α < 2a, so 2a-α is not a multiple of a. The same holds for every ka-α: (k-1)a < ka-α < ka. This includes a-α, which lies in (0, a).

§16. Hence every b that is not a multiple of a either satisfies b < a, or satisfies ka < b < (k+1)a for some k. This is the existence half of division with remainder: b = ka + r with 0 < r < a. Uniqueness is not stated.

§17. Examples.
- Multiples of 2 (here 2 itself included): 2, 4, 6, .... Every other number differs from one of them by 1.
- Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, .... Every other number is at distance 1 or 2 from one of them.
- These are the residue classes mod 2 and mod 3.

§18. Proof that 2a is a multiple of 2. Write a = 1+1+...+1 (a terms). Write it twice and add termwise: 2a = 2+2+...+2 (a terms). So 2a = a·2.

§19. Alternative phrasing: doubling a means taking each unit twice. This produces a collection of 2's, so 2a contains 2 exactly as often as a contains 1.

§20. Likewise 3a = 3+3+...+3 (a terms), so 3a is a multiple of 3. Euler asserts that the same holds for all multiples ('quod etiam de omnibus multiplis est intelligendum'). The general step is left to the reader.

§21. Definition: the index of a multiple is the number telling how many times it contains the simplum. The double has index 2, the triple index 3, and so on.

§22. Notation: a taken n times (as many times as n contains units) is written na, the multiple of a with index n.

§23. By the argument of §§18-20 (each unit of a replaced by n), na = n+n+...+n (a terms). So na is also the multiple of n with index a.

§24. Hence the multiple of a with index n coincides with the multiple of n with index a, i.e. na = an. This is commutativity of multiplication, proved by regrouping units, in effect counting an n×a array by rows or by columns.

§25. Because a and n can be interchanged, both are called 'factors', and na is called the 'product' ('productum seu factum').

§26. Every number is a multiple of 1 (with itself as index) and the simplum of itself (index 1). These trivial cases are henceforth excluded from the term 'multiple'. This prepares the definition of primes on the next page (§§27-35).
errors: §14-15 implicitly require α >= 1 (α = 0 would make every listed number a multiple). This is consistent with Euler's restriction to positive integers in §§1-6, but is not stated.
§16 asserts existence of the bracketing multiple without proof (it rests on the Archimedean/well-ordering property). Uniqueness of the quotient and remainder is not addressed.

§20 generalizes from the cases 2 and 3 to all indices by assertion ('quod etiam de omnibus multiplis est intelligendum'). §23-24 then rely on this general regrouping argument; there is no formal induction.
§17 counts 2 (and 3) among their own multiples ('ejus simplo non excluso'), departing explicitly from the convention of §11. Euler flags this himself, so it is not a slip.

§13: the phrase 'totidemque non-multipla' (a-1 non-multiples between consecutive multiples) is correct, but it presupposes the convention that a itself counts as a multiple for the gap between a and 2a.

results.what: Between consecutive multiples ka and (k+1)a there are exactly a-1 non-multiples; numbers ka±α with 0<α<a are not multiples of a
Every non-multiple b of a satisfies b<a or ka<b<(k+1)a
results.modern_name: Division algorithm (existence of quotient and remainder)

results.what: na = an proved by regrouping a units n-fold into a groups of n
results.modern_name: Commutativity of multiplication of natural numbers
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; rigorous inductive proof due to Grassmann (1861) / Dedekind / Peano

results.what: Definitions of index, factor and product; exclusion of trivial multiples (by 1 and by itself)
results.modern_name: Factors/product; nontrivial divisors (prelude to the definition of primes)

deep.surprise_reason: This is entirely elementary textbook arithmetic: multiples, remainders, and commutativity of multiplication by unit-counting. It belongs to Euler's well-known, already published (Opera Posthuma 1862) 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina'. Nothing is non-standard; the only mildly notable feature is that Euler proves na = an by an explicit counting argument rather than assuming it.

checkable.sympy: all((k*a + al) % a != 0 for a in range(2,30) for al in range(1,a) for k in range(0,20))
checkable.asserts: §14: ka+α (0<α<a) is never a multiple of a

checkable.sympy: all((k*a - al) % a != 0 for a in range(2,30) for al in range(1,a) for k in range(1,20))
checkable.asserts: §15: ka-α (0<α<a) is never a multiple of a

checkable.sympy: all(len([m for m in range(k*a+1,(k+1)*a) if m % a != 0]) == a-1 for a in range(2,30) for k in range(1,10))
checkable.asserts: §13: exactly a-1 non-multiples lie strictly between consecutive multiples

checkable.sympy: all(b < a or any(k*a < b < (k+1)*a for k in range(1, b)) for a in range(2,25) for b in range(1,200) if b % a != 0)
checkable.asserts: §16: a non-multiple is either below a or strictly between two consecutive multiples

checkable.sympy: all(min(n % 3, 3 - n % 3) in (1,2) for n in range(1,100) if n % 3 != 0)
checkable.asserts: §17: non-multiples of 3 are at distance 1 or 2 from a multiple of 3

checkable.sympy: all(sum([n]*a) == sum([a]*n) == n*a for a in range(1,30) for n in range(1,30))
checkable.asserts: §§18-24: a taken n times equals n taken a times (na = an)
